To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
caregivers of children on ART can accurately assess adherence, and that a small number of questions can be used to assess caregiver adherence.

we used a novel variable selection approach to identify the most informative items from a comprehensive adherence questionnaire, and that we identified items that were most informative for predicting caregiver-reported adherence to antiretovirals in children.
caregiver reports of missed doses, late doses, problems giving the medication, and caregiver-level items are the best predictors of antiretrovural therapy adherence among HIV-infected children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of a new tool for the assessment of adherence to antiretovirals in children with HIV/AIDS.
the identification of the best predictors for adherence to ART among HIV-infected children in western Kenya, which could be used in the design of adherence assessment tools for children.
the development of tools to measure and improve adherence to ART in HIV-infected children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the caregiver report of ART adherence is a good predictor of adherence in HIV-infected children.
the best way to assess adherence in pediatric patients is by using an objective measure, such as MEMS, as the gold standard.
the LASSO approach identified a subset of 9 of 48 caregiver report items that best predicted MEMS-measured ART adherence for HIV-infected children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we developed a novel approach using LASSO regression to identify items in a questionnaire that are most correlated with MEMS adherence and that these items are more strongly related to caregiver-reported adherence than other items.
we have identified a subset of adherence questions that can be used in future research to assess adherence in HIV-infected children.
caregiver-reported items can be used to assess pediatric ART adherence in low-resource settings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
caregiver-reported adherence is a valid measure of ART adherence among HIV-infected children.
the best predictors of pediatric adherence are not the same as for adult patients.
caregivers are able to provide accurate reports of their child’s adherence, but the items they are asked to report must be carefully selected.
